colon and rectal SCRCs show different genetic features associated with colon and rectal carcinogenesis.

the APC-β-cat pathway is the first hit in the development of SCRCs and that two pathways, one K-rass dependent and one K-rass independent, can be identified.
In summary, our research is concerned with
a better characterization of the genetic events leading to the development of SCRCs.
the identification of molecular pathways of colorectal carcinogenesis, and the results obtained can be used for the design of clinical trials.
the identification of the genetic alterations associated with colon and rectal carcinogenesis and their possible role in the pathogenesis of SCRCs.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
rectal cancer is more likely to be a different entity from colon cancer than colon cancer is likely to be from rectal cancer.
colon and rectal SCRCs can be considered as different entities.
colon and rectal carcinogenesis are two distinct entities.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

the APC gene is the most frequently affected gene in MIN− colon and rectal carcinogenesis, whereas the K-ras gene is the second hit in MIN− colon tumors, and the TP53 gene is the second mutation hit in MIN− rectal tumors.
the APC-TP53-chromosome 18q pathway is the most frequent pathway followed by SCRC development, and the APC-K-ras-chromosome 18-q pathway is the second most frequent pathway followed.
the APC-β-cat pathway is inactivated at the beginning of colon cancer, whereas rectal cancer develops along the APC-TP53 pathway.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the APC-β-caterin pathway is inactivating in most of SCRCs and that two preferential pathways are followed by SCRC, one K-rs dependent and the other K-Rs independent.
